(AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills) AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills America 250 Objects The Bagel A plain bagel with cream cheese is photographed in Phoenix, Ariz., Monday, July 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills) AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills ( 1 /4) Share This Gallery: Share This: share on facebook share on X share on threads share on linkedin share on email print NEW YORK (AP) — The bagel in America is an immigrant story with a hole in the middle. It came to America with Eastern European Jews escaping poverty and antisemitism. It landed in New York street carts and neighborhood bakeries. Later, it made its way to supermarket freezer aisles and into the breakfast order of so many every day. And like every food story, it starts with the first bite. As a layer of crunch prepares your brain for a crusty piece of bread, it’s immediately met by the soft yet dense chew of the inside. Eating the two textures together brings a feeling of joy, along with whatever toppings you’ve added. A schmear of cream cheese to keep it simple. A flavored spread to add a bit of zest. Or a bagel topped taller than the human mouth can handle with fish, tomato, cucumber and red onions. And we haven’t even talked about the flavor choices. A simple plain or egg bagel works for some (no judgment). Others insist on seeds — poppy, sesame — or shards of onion or salt. Others say it’s not a bagel unless it’s an everything, each bite snapping back at you with a different cascade of flavors. Purists will tell you to keep it simple. But with a bagel, like so much in American life, you can have it any way you’d like. The bagel started in Jewish communities in Poland and was brought here by Eastern European Jews escaping growing antisemitism in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. After arriving from Poland, Harry Lender worked at a New Jersey bakery to earn enough to bring his family to America. His sons grew the family’s work from their New Haven, Connecticut, bakery to supermarkets around the country with frozen bagels. The bagel, then, is another story of the success of immigrants in America. The shops that now sell them are run by families of those original immigrants and new groups who’ve come for a better life. But no matter how far the bagel spreads, it maintains a special place for American Jews. Many moments in the circle of life for Jews in America include boiled rings of dough stacked high to celebrate or eat away the grief. Ritual circumcision for a baby boy? Snip snip, then bagels for all. Bar mitzvah day 13 years later? Months of practice for an hour of work. Then: bagels. Shiva house mourning a loved one? “Sorry for your loss.” “Thank you. Bagels are in the other room.” In these situations, the bagel brings comfort — just as it has for generations of American Jews, immigrants, and anyone else looking for their place at the table. ___ Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. https://hungarytoday.hu/fidesz-kdnp-meps.text: Fidesz-KDNP MEPs Call for Immediate Release of EU Funds In a statement sent to MTI , the FIDESZ-KDNP (Christian Democratic People’s Party) members of the European Parliament are calling for the unconditional and immediate disbursement of the EU funds that the Orbán government negotiated for Hungary in 2020. The statement, released on Monday, noted that Tamás Deutsch, as a member of the European Parliament’s Committee on Budgets, proposed on behalf of the parliamentary group an increase of 11 billion euros in the EU budget for 2027. For political reasons, 55% of the funds—approximately 6.3 billion euros—for three Hungarian operational programs were frozen in 2022,” the statement reads. “The FIDESZ-KDNP Members of the European Parliament are demanding that not only the funds from the Recovery and Resilience Facility following the coronavirus pandemic, but also all of Hungary’s cohesion funds be disbursed to Hungary unconditionally and without delay,” the group of MEPs stated, adding: In December 2020, the delegation led by Viktor Orbán negotiated an additional 22 billion euros in cohesion funds for Hungary, on top of the funds from the Recovery Fund. The “liberal majority” in the European Commission and the European Parliament—which includes the TISZA Party—has withheld a portion of these funds “through political blackmail,” they wrote. They emphasize that the FIDESZ-KDNP proposal to increase the budget also includes a 2.5 billion euro increase in funding for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The Hungarian members of the Patriots for Europe group are calling for more funding to support young farmers, the wine sector, and beekeeping. They have reintroduced the proposal that the grand coalition of the People’s Party and The Left had previously rejected in the European Parliament’s Committee on Agriculture (AGRI): The EU crisis fund to compensate farmers is to be increased from the current 450 million euros to 900 million euros. The drought of the past few weeks has led to crop losses of 20 to 30% for grains and corn. But livestock farmers have also found themselves in a difficult situation: pastures have dried up, and feed prices have skyrocketed. For this reason as well, an increase in the crisis fund is urgently needed. Photo: MTI/Kocsis Zoltán The proposals put forward by the Hungarian delegation of the Patriots in the European Parliament call for cutting funding for the “misguided” EU migration policy by 1 billion euros and increasing spending on border protection by 2 billion euros, while explicitly demanding reimbursement of Hungary’s border protection costs. We demand that the migration pact, which was enforced unlawfully, be reviewed and withdrawn,” they state. The MEPs also make it clear that FIDESZ-KDNP—similar to last year—has proposed setting aside Erasmus funds for Hungarian universities undergoing a transition into a reserve until the European Commission disburses the funds to which the students are entitled. They note that it is well known that the European Commission has excluded a large portion of Hungarian students from participating in the Erasmus program. “Contrary to the election promises of the TISZA government, it has failed to put an end to this outrageous situation,” the delegation states, adding: “The members of the patriotic faction therefore continue to demand that the European Commission immediately reverse its decision affecting Hungarian students.” They also demand an end to the ideologically motivated political blackmail of member states; for this reason, we would cut 250 million euros from the EU budget allocated to support left-wing civil society organizations, the FIDESZ-KDNP parliamentary group added in its statement. https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/oct.text: ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan: ‘We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability.’ Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters View image in fullscreen ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan: ‘We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability.’ Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters International criminal court ICC prosecutor says court making ‘significant progress’ despite US sanctions Nazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffected Julian Borger Senior international correspondent Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.35 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 09.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The deputy prosecutor of the international criminal court has said new US sanctions are beginning to take effect on its staff but insisted they have not hindered the court’s work. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the sanctions this month , accusing the ICC – a frequent target of the Trump administration – of being a “rogue court” and declaring: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” Nazhat Shameem Khan, who is co-running the office pending the appointment of a new chief prosecutor, said the court was so far continuing its work. She said the Gaza war investigation and others had made “significant progress” since war crimes arrest warrants were issued in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister, Yoav Galant. Further applications from the prosecutor were being kept secret by order of the court, she said. View image in fullscreen The ICC issued a war crimes arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters Some ICC staff had however encountered banking problems, she said, even though the US sanctions on the court were not due to take effect until six months from 9 October, the date of their announcement. She said the banks were “over-complying” to minimise risk while there was uncertainty over the ultimate scope of the measures. “These are sanctions imposed on the institutions and, in principle, our individual members should not be impacted directly,” the Fijian deputy prosecutor said in an interview with the Guardian. “But again, what I am hearing from members of our staff is that some of them are experiencing difficulties in banking.” The court is working on insulating itself from sanctions imposed by a hostile administration in Washington. It has switched its software from Microsoft to European ​alternatives, and is negotiating with relevant service providers over banking and health insurance. “All the investigations across all situations continue. We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability or reduce our output,” Khan said, acknowledging that it was impossible to anticipate the full impact of sanctions when they officially took effect. The new sanctions target the whole institution of the ICC, but the US first targeted 13 ICC staff in February 2025. Khan was one of them, so is accustomed to dealing with sanctions, which affect aspects of everyday life. “Life without a credit card is inconvenient. It’s amazing how many things now we cannot do around the world, particularly in relation to travel, without a credit card,” she said, but added that her inconvenience was put into perspective when she visited refugee camps or sites of mass atrocities. “We see the faces of our victims for whom sanctions and credit cards are completely irrelevant. They just want justice.” View image in fullscreen The former ICC chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters American sanctions are not the only disruption to the ICC prosecutors’ work. Formal investigations began in late November 2024 into allegations of sexual harassment against the former chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. The British jurist (who is no relation to the deputy prosecutor) denied the charges. He was removed in July this year after a vote by member states. No further charges over the Gaza war have been announced since late 2024. Khan insisted that investigative work on the Israel-Palestine file had only gone quiet because of the court’s ruling earlier this year that all charges and applications for warrants should be kept secret until the judges decide they can be made public. “Even if we reach a stage of the investigations where it might be imminent, we may not discuss it publicly,” she said. “And so while there might be an appearance that nothing is happening, I can assure you that there’s significant progress in that particular situation as well as others.” When announcing the sanctions, Rubio gave the ICC a six-month grace period “to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns” but it is unclear what would satisfy the Trump administration , which has exhibited a longstanding hostility towards the court. Rubio claimed, without evidence, this month that “globalist ‘experts’ an ocean away” wanted the ICC to prosecute US citizens. Khan said it was unclear who and what Rubio had in mind. View image in fullscreen US secretary of state, Marco Rubio: ‘Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.’ Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters/AP “It is possible that there is a mistaken belief on the part of those who are concerned that we are pursuing Americans, but we certainly haven’t brought any Americans before the court,” she said. “If his reference is to Afghanistan, then in fact the priority for the investigation is in relation to offences committed specifically against women, girls and other vulnerable groups by the Taliban and by the Islamic State Khorasan in Afghanistan.” This month, four arrest warrants were unsealed by the ICC pretrial chamber against members of the Taliban on charges of gender persecution. The court registrar for the ICC is in negotiation with the EU over blocking the US sanctions or protecting the court in other ways. There has been support for the court, and on Thursday, the European parliament awarded its Sakharov prize for freedom of thought to the court and its officials. Khan said the support was “a very important message that the staff at the court need to hear”, as were pledges from other countries to continue to contribute towards the ICC’s costs. “I think that the fact that there is so much attention on us is a reflection of how relevant we are,” Khan said. “This is a court that provides an avenue of justice for victims who have nowhere else to go, who really want to cut past politics and want their voices to be heard.” Explore more on these topics International criminal court International criminal justice Trump administration Marco Rubio US politics Israel-Gaza war US foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text: California FDR made it a blue bastion – now it’s Trump’s stronghold in California. Is it forever lost? Shasta has embraced the Maga movement with gusto – can Democrats ever win back the rural, working-class voters they once relied upon? Dani Anguiano in Shasta county Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.02 EDT Share View image in fullscreen Pat Carr looks through photographs at his home in Cottonwood, California. Photograph: Mason Trinca/Mason Trinca for The Guardian A crucial election was approaching and the country was desperate. Despite promises that economic conditions were improving, nearly a quarter of the US was out of work as voters headed to the polls in 1932. It was the darkest time since the civil war, a period so dire that in California’s capital people fought each other for work. In early 1931, a crowd of 200 men scuffled over a handful of temporary jobs moving back-breaking loads of granite, the Sacramento Bee reported. That same newspaper urged its readers to find odd jobs to save fellow citizens from hunger and homelessness. Those who had already lost shelter set up along the banks of the Sacramento River, as unhoused people would do decades later , and were, in some cases, near starvation, according to the Bee. The situation was often even worse in the remote and rural communities further up north, where opportunities were fewer and relief was slower. In Shasta county, which stretches from the northernmost reaches of the Central Valley to the state’s dense forests, residents were struggling. View image in fullscreen Loggers move timber using horses and ‘big wheel’ wagons near Mount Shasta in this 1930 photograph. A ‘donkey’ steam engine can be seen in the background. Photograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty Images Shasta had been founded in 1850, as hundreds of thousands flocked to California in search of gold. The region became a productive center for gold mining, with newcomers scouring creeks and boring through mountains in search of the precious metal. It was a place of opportunity, a soon to be railroad hub that offered jobs in copper mining, agriculture and the timber industries. Then came the depression. In one mountain town, a group of jobless men were accused of setting a blaze with the aim of being hired to extinguish it. Desperate people returned to the green hills that once yielded fortunes, hoping to find a bit of gold again. “Not getting rich, but I dug out $18.90 last month,” one young man told a reporter in 1931. “I eat, and that beats being jobless and hungry.” Franklin Delano Roosevelt promised hope and help. He traveled to 41 states during his campaign, making a point to visit small towns and rural areas. When he stopped in Redding, the Shasta county seat, in September 1932, businesses closed and classes ended early so that everyone could see the New York governor’s remarks. “I am not making this trip a political one. I am making it to learn the conditions and needs of every section of the United States,” he told a crowd of several thousand from the back of a train. “We are not making this fight against the Republican party but against Republican leadership which has brought the country to its present condition.” View image in fullscreen Franklin D Roosevelt speaks from the rear of a train alongside his daughter Anna in Redding in 1932. Photograph: National Archives and Records Administration His message resonated. Despite Republican insistence that the party would carry California, the state went, as one newspaper declared, “Democratic and progressive with a vengeance”. That was especially true in Shasta, where just over 72% of voters backed Roosevelt. Nearly a century later, it’s an election result that is difficult to imagine. Shasta is the de facto Maga capital of California, and a center of the US election denial movement. Roughly two-thirds of voters supported Donald Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. They took his political philosophy and ran with it, electing officials who promoted falsehoods about stolen elections and frequently clashed with the state. During the pandemic, the area drew national attention for its hostility to Covid restrictions. The years that followed brought more turmoil that touched all corners of public life, documented in headline after headline – a journalist assaulted while covering a meeting of local conservative groups, a protester who faced jail time for holding a sign calling for the resignation of an elected official during a public meeting. Map of 2024 presidential political results in northern California. Shasta county, with a republican majority, is highlighted. For more than a year, the Guardian has explored the political transformation that unfolded here over the 20th century. The story that emerged through conversations with longtime residents, historians, and political experts is one of a community that dramatically veered right amid the collapse of its major industries and became a hotbed for radical conservative politics. And it’s a chapter in the story of the Democratic party. Shasta can be seen as a case study for how the Democrats have struggled to regain a crucial pillar of the base they once relied upon – rural America – even as they appear on track to win back crucial seats this midterm election. The small settlement of Cottonwood is perhaps best known for its rugged western beauty, nearby fish hatchery and rightwing militia. It is a place of wide open spaces with sprawling cattle ranches and pristine views of the junction of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades. Even in a deeply Republican county, the community stands apart for its conservatism. Along the roads, underneath majestic oaks, are old signs for measure B, a controversial ballot initiative voters approved in June that would end nearly all voting by mail while requiring voter ID and a hand count. The effort put the county in yet another legal battle with the state – a judge blocked the measure from taking effect as the litigation moves ahead. View image in fullscreen Cattle graze in a pasture near Cottonwood, with Lassen Peak in the distance. Photograph: Mason Trinca/The Guardian A few miles away, inside a packed home office not far from the Sacramento River, Pat Carr has assembled a sort of museum showcasing a mostly forgotten history. Old photos of local luminaries with Democratic presidents line the walls, along with letters from White House officials and even a supreme court justice. The documents paint a portrait of a deep blue region built by Democratic policies. “When I try to explain that to people here now, they’re going, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me. It couldn’t have been like that’,” Carr, 82, said sitting in front of a table crowded with memorabilia. “Those of us that remember a heyday, we’re almost all dead.” In the 20th century, Shasta residents played crucial roles in state and federal politics. They chaired California’s Democratic party, helped bring major infrastructure projects to the region, and they served in John F Kennedy’s administration. Carr knows the history well – it was his family’s. In a photo of Roosevelt’s Redding visit, FDR stands alongside Carr’s grandfather, Francis. Carr’s father and cousin managed Kennedy’s Northern California campaign, and his uncle was the undersecretary of the interior department under Kennedy. View image in fullscreen Pat Carr at home in Cottonwood. Photograph: Mason Trinca/Mason Trinca for The Guardian “The money was flowing out of Washington into the north state, and the guys that were getting it done were all Democrats,” Carr recalls. The Shasta Dam is a 600ft tall monument to that era. Constructed with 15m tons of concrete, with a reservoir capable of holding back some 4.5m acre-feet of dark green water, the dam has helped make California an agricultural powerhouse as the keystone of the Central Valley Project. It sends vast quantities of water from the state’s far north to more arid sections of the Central Valley for farming, and generates enough electricity to power as many as 710,000 homes. The federal government, which manages it, considers the dam critical infrastructure at a level just below the White House and the Pentagon, a tour guide said on a September morning. During its construction amid the Great Depression and through the second world war, it provided thousands of badly needed jobs. Roosevelt came to the White House with broad support and implemented an ambitious agenda that over his first term helped build a powerful coalition of labor unions, African Americans, the working class, liberal professionals and white southerners that became the backbone of his party. Mere months after he took office, there were work camps established in Shasta county through the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). View image in fullscreen The Shasta Dam. Photograph: Mike Kai Chen/The Guardian The president’s administration put millions of Americans to work through programs such as the CCC, which enlisted jobless young men to build campgrounds, cut firelines and construct fire lookouts. The agencies he created worked in virtually every county in the US, helped bring power to vast swaths of the country, and established much of the local infrastructure we now know. Redding, the largest city in the area, received federal dollars to build a fire station, post office, bridge and veterans memorial building. “That won over the hearts of millions of ordinary people,” said Richard Walker, a professor emeritus at UC Berkeley and the director of the Living New Deal research project. “They felt that the government cared. Critically, they felt they participated. They were helping their own community, whether it was fixing streets and sidewalks or planting trees or building schools.” The county had scored the most significant investment in the form of the dam, one of the largest public works projects of the era and one of the most important hydroelectric facilities in the world at the time, Walker said. View image in fullscreen Construction workers of the site of the Shasta Dam, circa 1940. Photograph: Frederic Lewis/Getty Images Most of California’s water is located in the north, while 80% of the demand lies in the central and southern regions of the state. For decades, California had sought a solution to the imbalance and the winter flooding of valley communities. The state couldn’t afford to finance the project during the depression, but after lobbying from prominent Californians including Francis Carr, Roosevelt’s administration funded it. “Things are more optimistic than ever before in [the] Central Valley. We are delighted with prospects of immediate work,” state senator John B McColl said in 1937 before construction began. It employed almost 5,000 people at one time – bringing new residents. Construction was under way 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and was considered so vital that some workers received draft deferments during the second world war. The dam translated into enduring Democratic loyalty, said Bob Mulholland, a veteran Democratic strategist and longtime resident of northern California. “I think there was a certain amount of that commitment or thanks for years, from the workers themselves and the kids, to FDR and the Democrats,” Mulholland said in an interview with the Guardian in 2025 shortly before his death. The war brought significant growth in the timber industry, as did surging demand for housing in the years that followed. It was an era of opportunity and expansion in this part of the state, with ample jobs in the mills and unions for wide swaths of workers from loggers to retail clerks to bartenders. It echoed what was happening across the US. “After the war, the United States experienced the greatest economic boom in human history and moreover, even as inequality was declining, the rich were still getting richer,” said historian Harvey Kaye, a professor emeritus of democracy and justice at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay. “Everyone was doing better.” View image in fullscreen The agencies Roosevelt created established much of the local infrastructure we now know. Redding, the largest city in the area, received federal dollars to build a veterans memorial building, a fire station, and a post office. Photograph: Mike Kai Chen/The Guardian By 1948, when Diane Kinyon was born, Shasta was one of California’s bluest counties and an important part of its Democratic base. Kinyon’s family had migrated to the area in the 1860s and for generations worked in the industries that helped build and feed California, from the railroad to ranching and logging. Her parents were “diehard Democrats”, she said. Her father, a union man, was employed by the county road department, working his way up after starting as a mechanic, and also owned a pizza shop with her mother. Her father emphasized the importance of unions to Kinyon who later who spent decades as a union organizer. “We knew we were union. We knew we were Democrats, and we knew what that meant was that you help people,” she recalled. “But I think on the other side, [those were Republican] values too. They just financially had a different way to get there.” In the 1960s, the construction of Interstate 5, the nearly 1,400-mile (about 2,253km) highway that runs from Mexico to Canada, opened up the county, and brought more tourists, Kinyon recalled. Road work, along with reservoir projects, offered even more jobs. The region’s extractive industries created challenges over the years – pollution from the mining industry damaged crops, seeped into waterways and poisoned fish. Still, a sense of hope hung over the region, along with near constant smoke from wood waste burners at the mills, recalled Pat Carr and his brother Jeff, a farmer and retired teacher. It was a sweet wood smell rather than the acrid wildfire smoke California frequently endures today. The industry was in full swing in 1960, when Kennedy ran for president, and Shasta was still a Democratic powerhouse. Kennedy visited the area twice, following the same trail as Harry Truman in 1948, he said on one visit. He spoke in Redding in 1960, praising the Shasta Dam and telling the crowd “water is key to the American future” and that “this valley shows what can be done”. Shasta went on to have some of the highest support for Kennedy of any county in the state. And James Kennedy Carr, the Carr brothers’ uncle, became the undersecretary of the department of the interior. View image in fullscreen President Kennedy with James K Carr, then undersecretary of the interior, in this 1962 photograph. The photograph is inscribed ‘JFK and JKC — Two fine ones!’ and signed by then interior secretary Stewart Udall. Photograph: Courtesy of Pat Carr While the US benefited from the legacy of the New Deal, major changes would soon alter the Democratic party and fracture the coalition Roosevelt built. The successes of the civil rights movement and the Democrats’ support of landmark legislation resulted in many white southerners beginning to abandon the party. Lyndon Johnson was the last Democratic presidential candidate to attract support from a majority of white Americans. Meanwhile, conservatives and the corporate elite began what historian Kaye describes as a class war and crusade against the achievements of the “long age of Roosevelt”. Business groups touted “free enterprise” in an effort to disempower unions and reduce government regulation, while corporations moved operations to the US south and abroad to cut costs and skirt regulations, Kaye has argued . Jimmy Carter embraced deregulation and austerity measures, Kaye said, and his policies ultimately weakened unions. “The Democratic party basically turned its back on the working class,” Kaye said. “Republicans benefited from the Democrats abandoning the FDR tradition and the age of Roosevelt that had made them the majority party of the people from the early 1930s right through the early 70s.” Shasta remained reliably blue for a little lo

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/ue/f.text: Cancelarul german Friedrich Merz condiționează un acord privind viitorul buget multianual al Uniunii Europene de asumarea unui nou angajament financiar pentru Ucraina, în valoare de aproximativ 45 de miliarde de euro. Berlinul cere ca toate statele membre să contribuie la acoperirea deficitului bugetar al Kievului, însă propunerea riscă să adâncească diviziunile dintre țările care susțin finanțarea comună și cele care se opun unor noi împrumuturi pentru Ucraina, potrivit Euronews . Kievul se confruntă cu un deficit bugetar de aproximativ 70 de miliarde de euro pentru anul 2027, pe fondul războiului și al atacurilor aeriene neîncetate ale Rusiei. Uniunea Europeană și-a asumat să acopere două treimi din această sumă, adică aproximativ 45 de miliarde de euro, printr-un mecanism de finanțare care urmează să fie stabilit. „Un angajament colectiv prin care noi toți, fără excepție, să contribuim în mod echitabil la acoperirea acestui deficit este o condiție prealabilă esențială pentru rezolvarea acestei probleme și pentru discutarea oricăror alte chestiuni, în special a celor cu implicații financiare”, a declarat Merz într-o scrisoare adresată președintelui Consiliului European, Antonio Costa, consultată de Euronews. Cancelarul german susține că negocierile privind bugetul multianual al Uniunii, care acoperă o perioadă de șapte ani, trebuie să asigure „o soluție susținută de toate statele membre, care să garanteze o perspectivă de finanțare solidă și multianuală pentru Ucraina începând cu 2028, inclusiv obligațiile de plată a dobânzilor care s-au acumulat deja”. Dobânzile la care face referire Merz sunt aferente împrumutului de sprijin în valoare de 90 de miliarde de euro, finanțat prin împrumuturi comune contractate de 24 de state membre. Ungaria, Slovacia și Republica Cehă au obținut o derogare de la participarea la acest mecanism, în schimbul asigurării unanimității necesare pentru aprobarea sa. Principalul împrumutului nu va trebui rambursat până când Rusia nu va accepta să plătească despăgubiri de război. În schimb, plățile dobânzilor vor începe să devină scadente de anul viitor. Inițial, Comisia Europeană estima costurile la aproximativ trei miliarde de euro anual, însă creșterea bruscă a costurilor de împrumut a modificat calculele. Cele 45 de miliarde de euro pe care UE intenționează să le acorde Ucrainei în 2027 ar urma să se adauge împrumutului existent. Având în vedere amploarea deficitului financiar al Kievului, o nouă rundă de împrumuturi comune a devenit rapid opțiunea preferată. Comisia Europeană urmează să prezinte statelor membre variantele posibile înaintea unui summit special programat la sfârșitul lunii. În scrisoarea adresată lui António Costa, Merz îi cere să accelereze calendarul discuțiilor și să includă finanțarea Ucrainei printre „prioritățile” summitului informal de la Dublin, organizat în această săptămână. Subiectul nu figura inițial pe ordinea de zi. Cancelarul german critică în mod explicit faptul că sprijinul financiar și militar acordat Ucrainei, o țară epuizată de război, este „distribuit inegal și suportat în mare parte doar de câteva state membre”. „Sprijinirea Ucrainei este o chestiune care ține de securitatea noastră europeană indivizibilă, la fel trebuie să fie și împărțirea sarcinilor pentru acest sprijin”, a scris Merz. Germania este cel mai mare donator bilateral al Ucrainei. Alte state care susțin Kievul, printre care Danemarca, Finlanda, Țările de Jos și Suedia, împărtășesc nemulțumirile Berlinului și vor ca bugetul UE și finanțarea Ucrainei să fie negociate în cadrul aceluiași pachet. Aceste țări fac parte din grupul așa-numiților „frugali” sau „modernizatori”, care pledează pentru reduceri generale ale cheltuielilor prevăzute în proiectul de buget european. Poziția lor le pune în opoziție cu „Prietenii coeziunii”, grupul de state care susține menținerea unui nivel ridicat al finanțării pentru politicile de coeziune. Republica Cehă, Ungaria și Slovacia au transmis că nu intenționează să participe la un nou mecanism de împrumut comun destinat sprijinirii Ucrainei. Bulgaria, un critic vehement al livrărilor de arme către Kiev, este așteptată să adopte o poziție similară. Cele patru state fac parte din grupul „Prietenii coeziunii”. Refuzul lor de a participa la finanțarea comună a provocat nemulțumirea țărilor care susțin o împărțire mai echitabilă a costurilor. „Tabăra coeziunii nu poate să aibă totul”, a declarat un diplomat european. „La Bruxelles nu există un copac cu bani, așa că trebuie să facem alegeri politice.” Simon Harris, ministrul irlandez de Finanțe, a cărui țară deține președinția rotativă a Consiliului UE și coordonează negocierile, s-a alăturat poziției susținute de grupul „frugalilor”. „Este foarte greu să purtăm o discuție serioasă despre bugetul european pentru următorii ani fără a lua în considerare Ucraina și finanțarea acesteia”, a declarat Harris luni dimineață, înainte de a participa la o reuniune ministerială la Bruxelles. Este vorba, de fapt, de securitatea europeană”, a adăugat oficialul irlandez. Nu toate statele membre sunt însă de acord cu legarea celor două dosare. Ignacy Niemczycki, viceministrul polonez responsabil cu afacerile europene, a susținut săptămâna trecută că finanțarea Ucrainei și negocierile privind bugetul UE sunt chestiuni fundamental diferite. În opinia sa, asocierea lor ar putea „avea efecte negative” și ar face ca obținerea unui acord final să fie „și mai dificilă” decât în prezent. La rândul său, premierul slovac Robert Fico a avertizat că o asemenea legătură între cele două dosare ar fi „foarte periculoasă”. Disputa riscă astfel să complice negocierile privind viitorul buget al Uniunii Europene, într-un moment în care statele membre trebuie să ajungă la un compromis atât asupra priorităților de cheltuieli, cât și asupra modului în care va fi finanțat sprijinul pentru Ucraina.
